data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel’s Netanyahu accused of attempting coup after election defeat
data.author: Nadav Rapaport
data.summary:
Israel’s Netanyahu accused of attempting coup after election defeat
Submitted by
Nadav Rapaport
on
Thu, 11/05/2026 - 14:28
Opposition figures and commentators say prime minister is using Shin Bet to overturn election result and cling to power
An aide speaks to Benjamin Netanyahu as he gives a statement following exit polls for Israel's national election, in Jerusalem, 28 October 2026 (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Off
Israeli politicians and commentators have accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of attempting a coup after his election defeat last week, which followed a historic turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
They say he is using the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic intelligence agency, to undermine the result and retain power.
More than a week after the results showed the Netanyahu-led bloc trailing the opposition, Shin Bet chief David Zini is reportedly leading investigations into the Palestinian vote. The inquiries have raised allegations of voting fraud, bribery and foreign interference, despite no evidence being made public.
The investigations coincide with Netanyahu’s campaign to delegitimise the Palestinian-led parties Ra’am and the Joint List, which together secured an unprecedented 19 seats in the Knesset. Critics say the effort is aimed at keeping him in power.
On Tuesday, the Shin Bet arrested Middle East Eye contributor Abd Abu Shahadeh, citing a “security-related investigation”. Israeli media reported that Zini also wants Palestinian political leaders Ahmad Tibi, Sami Abou Shahadeh, Mansour Abbas and Ayman Odeh questioned.
Yair Golan, leader of the opposition Democrats party, warned on Wednesday that Israeli democracy was under threat.
“The police are detaining political activists without a warrant. The Shin Bet is trying to question senior elected officials without presenting evidence. The outgoing government refuses to recognise the election results,” he said.
Golan later accused Netanyahu of trying to “carry out a coup and seize power by force”.

Saudi coalition says it intercepted missile fired at Medina
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis on Thursday said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the group at the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest cities.
The announcement came just minutes after the kingdom's civil defence agency warned of potential danger in the area near the strategic port of Yanbu.
It was unclear if the two events were connected.
"Air defence intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Medina region," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a post on X.
The Houthis rejected any suggestion they were targeting the city, saying such accusations were a "blatant and grave falsehood".
"Our operations target only its oil facilities and military bases," the group said in a statement.

data.author: Bilge Kotan

Arab-led Joint List says it will back Eisenkot to form Israel's next government
The Arab-led Joint List has said it will back Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a new government, dealing a heavy blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's efforts to remain in power.
The Joint List announced on Thursday that it would "recommend that Gadi Eisenkot be tasked with forming the government", bringing the total number of lawmakers backing him to 67 in the 120-seat Knesset.
The decision follows Wednesday's endorsement by Ra'am, another Arab-led party, whose eight lawmakers also backed Eisenkot.
The two parties together secured a record 19 seats in last week's general election, giving them a potentially decisive role in determining who forms Israel's next government.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli settlers move into homes near West Bank city
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Israeli settlers move into homes near West Bank city
Israeli settlers moved into houses they say they purchased near the occupied West Bank city of Jericho this week, while Palestinian officials say the sale documents were forged.
An AFP reporter saw families with children moving into homes on the outskirts of the ancient city in the West Bank.
Palestinians fear that the new settlement outpost could bring an increased army presence and settler violence.
Several Palestinian communities in the greater Jericho area have already been driven from their homes by harassment from settlers over the past year.
The Israeli families moved into eight houses just outside Jericho's city limits on Wednesday, Hanan Greenwood, a settler representative, told AFP, near the ancient site known as the Hasmonean Palaces.
Hussein Hamayel, governor of the Jericho region, told AFP that the land in question is owned by the Palestinian Authority and cannot be sold.
"What is being promoted is a forgery, not a sale, and what is being circulated is settler propaganda," Hamayel said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: ICJ is due to rule on the Rohingya genocide case. Here's what you need to know
data.author: Sondos Asem
data.summary:
ICJ is due to rule on the Rohingya genocide case. Here's what you need to know
Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Thu, 11/05/2026 - 11:06
UN's top court sets 19 November as date for landmark judgment in case brought by Gambia against Myanmar
Off
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, in a judgment that could see the court hold a state responsible for genocide for the first time.
Officials announced on Tuesday that the court's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, would read the judgment at a public sitting at the Peace Palace in The Hague at 10am local time on 19 November.
The ruling will be final and binding, with no right of appeal.
Several governments have already described the violence as genocide, including the US and Canada.
Legal experts say they expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.
The case, brought by the Gambia in 2019, concerns the Myanmar military's 2017 violence in Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh and involved widely documented massacres and rapes.
About 1.2 million Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority, now live in camps around Cox's Bazar, the world's largest refugee settlement.
Myanmar has denied committing genocide, saying its forces were responding to insurgents from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa), whose attacks on police posts in August 2017 killed 12 security personnel.
Antonia Mulvey, an international human rights lawyer who investigated sexual violence against the Rohingya for the UN in 2017, told Middle East Eye's Expert Witness Podcast that horrific sexual violence was central to the Gambia's argument that genocide took place.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Palestine Action ban appeal enters closed proceedings at UK Supreme Court
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Palestine Action ban appeal enters closed proceedings at UK Supreme Court
The appeal against the ban on Palestine Action entered closed proceedings at the UK Supreme Court on Thursday, after the government and lawyers representing the group's co-founder concluded their public arguments, paving the way for judges to hear secret evidence presented by the government.
Opening the proceedings, James Eadie KC, representing the Home Office, disputed claims that Palestine Action "stood within the long tradition of civil disobedience in Britain".
"Their activities are planned and undertaken secretly in order to avoid detection," Eadie said, adding that they caused "serious damage to property".
Reiterating that the court should defer to parliament's decision to ban Palestine Action, Eadie argued that the direct-action group's track record of property damage to Israeli weapons met the legal definition of terrorism.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Aipac spent $55m on losing congressional candidates in midterm elections: Report
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Aipac spent $55m on losing congressional candidates in midterm elections: Report
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) spent more than $84m in the 2026 US midterms, but nearly two-thirds of those funds were spent on losing candidates, according to a new report from Responsible Statecraft.
Aipac’s Super Pac and other groups spent $55m on failed candidates. The largest portion of those funds, about $32m, was spent trying to defeat Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.
The results marked one of Aipac’s worst performances in years, suggesting that the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has contributed to soaring cost-of-living issues, resonated strongly with voters.
In the 2022 midterms, Aipac’s Super Pac, United Democracy Project, saw 69 percent of its expenditure spent on races backed by the organisation that won. That number was even higher in 2024, after Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with 87 percent of its spending going to successful races.
